title: Portrait of a Gurmukh

cards: Some people walk into a tense room and it settles a little. The arguing quiets. Somebody gets offered a chair.

The kid in the corner gets noticed. They don't announce anything; nobody remembers what they said, only that things went better. The Sikh tradition has a word for a person living like that at their best: gurmukh.
And for the opposite: manmukh. For weeks this path has taken the virtues one at a time. Today they sit together for a single portrait.

teach.h: A FACE TURNED TOWARD THE GURU.
teach.b: First, the word. Sikhs explain gurmukh as one whose face is turned toward the Guru, and manmukh as one turned toward their own mind. The difference isn't talent, or family, or how much scripture someone knows.
It's direction. Second, the portrait. Gather the traits from these weeks and a likeness appears.
Humble: strength that doesn't need to show. Truthful: in speech, and in conduct when nobody's checking. Content: at peace with what is, and still working.
Serving: hands in the langar, at the shoe stand, with the dishes. Remembering: the Name under the breath, all through the day. Third, the text.
A pauri of the Japji says, in paraphrase: through the Guru comes the sound of the Word; through the Guru comes wisdom; through the Guru, the One is found everywhere.
Gurmukh naadan, gurmukh vedan. Here gurmukh is less a title than a doorway. Wisdom arrives by turning.
Fourth, a portrait you grow into. Sikhs speak of becoming gurmukh, not of being born one, and they speak of it as grace and effort together. Nobody holds the whole likeness on a bad day.
A portrait isn't a mirror that judges.
It's a direction to face, again and again, like a sunflower turning through the day.

how: Sikhs describe the gurmukh, one turned toward the Guru, as the ideal of the Sikh life: humble, truthful, content, serving others and remembering the Name; it is spoken of as something one grows into by grace and effort.

games.q: what does “portrait of a gurmukh” mean?
o: a scholar who knows the scripture by heart
a person whose face is turned toward the Guru
a person born into a devout Sikh family

p: strength that doesn't need to show

s: gurmukh and manmukh are a matter of talent
it's direction: toward the Guru, or toward one's own mind.
the Japji uses the word gurmukh
gurmukh naadan, gurmukh vedan: through the Guru, the Word and wisdom.
Sikhs speak of being born gurmukh
they speak of becoming gurmukh, by grace and effort together.

games.q: a friend says: i could never be a gurmukh. i lose my temper, and i forget to pray. what does the portrait point toward?
o: agree; some people are simply born that way.
turn toward it again, one trait at a time.
games.why: Sikhs speak of becoming gurmukh by grace and effort. the portrait is a direction to face, again and again.

practice: Let the traits pass by slowly, one per breath: humble, truthful, content, serving, remembering. Notice which one feels farthest away today, not the easiest but the one that tugs, and breathe with it.
Picture one moment where it could live, a meeting where someone else gets the credit, a dish you wash that isn't yours, and if you pray, hold that moment before God.

wordCard.voice: Portrait of a Gurmukh. One whose face is turned toward the Guru: humble, truthful, content, serving, remembering, and still growing. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: one turned toward the Guru; the opposite is ਮਨਮੁਖ, manmukh.

carryVoice: Your line: grow into it. Nobody is born holding the whole likeness. Go gently.

sources.ref: Ang 2 (Japji, pauri 5: gurmukh naadan gurmukh vedan)
